It is inserted into the P-loop nucleotide-binding domain: in 1vdz the catalytic core is d1vdza1 (c.37.1.11, extended AAA-ATPase, discontinuous A:60-113 + A:191-439), the bulge is d1vdza2 (b.84.5.1, A:114-190) and the C-terminal helical domain is d1vdza3 (a.69.1.2).

Why a separate superfamily rather than a family inside an existing one: SCOP/SCOPe places domains in the same superfamily only when structure plus sequence, functional or other evidence indicates probable common ancestry. The other four b.84 superfamilies are b.84.1 Single hybrid motif (biotinyl/lipoyl carrier domains, 7-8 strands in two sheets), b.84.2 Rudiment single hybrid motif, b.84.3 Duplicated hybrid motif (8-strand half-barrel sandwiched with two 3-stranded sheets) and b.84.4 Ribosomal L27 protein-like (a permuted-topology rudiment hybrid). Each is held together by a conserved function or a recognised motif/duplication relationship. The ~75-residue bulge shares only the gross architecture of the fold (curator comment on b.84: "sandwich of half-barrel shaped beta-sheets"); it has no detectable sequence similarity to any of them, is not a carrier/lipoyl-type domain, has a different functional role (an insertion unique to V/A-type catalytic A subunits that is absent from the F1 beta subunit and contacts the B subunit and peripheral stalk), and has an independent evolutionary history as an insertion into a c.37.1 ATPase core. The superfamily annotation cites only PubMed 19893485 (the T. thermophilus V1 A3B3 structure paper) rather than any homology argument. Hence the curators (this superfamily was newly created in SCOPe 2.06; it does not exist in SCOP 1.75 or SCOPe 2.05) grouped the bulge with the barrel-sandwich hybrids only at the fold level.

Within b.84.5 the claim is stronger: the archaeal A1 (Pyrococcus) and bacterial/eukaryotic V1 (Thermus, yeast) bulge domains are orthologous, i.e. a single family of clearly related sequences descended from a common V/A-type A-subunit ancestor.
